" <p> It is the " persistent warmth " of the past few months that has led to summer 2025 outranking 1976 and all others in terms of overall average temperature , the Met Office added . <p> Climate change " continues to play a role " , with the UK warming at a rate of approximately 0.25C per decade . <p> The figures also show that an average of 212.1mm of rain fell across the UK over June , July and August , which is around 84% of the long-term seasonal trend . <p> This is some way above the driest summer on record in 1995 , when 105.9mm was measured . <p> But it follows directly after the driest spring in the UK since 1974 and the second driest seen in England since Met Office rainfall data began in 1836 . <p> Central , southern and eastern parts of England and Wales had an " especially dry " summer , while north-western parts of the UK , particularly Scotland , were much wetter . <p> Dr Mark McCarthy , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ : " Our analysis shows that the summer of 2025 has been made much more likely because of the greenhouse gases humans have released since the industrial revolution . <p> " In a natural climate , we could expect to see a summer like 2025 with an approximate return period of around 340 years , while in the current climate we could expect to see these sorts of summers roughly one in every five years . <p> " Another interesting finding from our analysis is the context of this summer against other record-breaking summers , like that of 1976 . <p> " Our analysis suggests that while 2025 has set a new record , we could plausibly experience much hotter summers in our current and near-future climate and shows how what would have been seen as extremes in the past are becoming more common in our changing climate " .

@@128782968 <h> James Hepburne Scott obituary : forestry expert <p> Forestry expert who oversaw the planting of 13 million trees to offset carbon emissions and played the violin in a reels band , dies aged 78 <p> The Times <p> Monday September 01 2025 , 12.01am , The Times <p> Hepburne Scott went to Sandhurst where he was on par for the Sword of Honour <p> PHIL WILKINSON <p> The Times <p> Monday September 01 2025 , 12.01am , The Times <p> Planting trees to save the planet is now such a familiar idea that few doubt the contribution it can make in battling climate change . In the 1990s , however , as the UK government withdrew tax incentives , woodland creation was falling steeply , and by 2008 had reached its lowest level for 30 years . James Hepburne Scott , balancing a career in forestry with political ambitions , realised that if a means could be found of encouraging the investment of private capital in the capture of carbon , then the decline in new planting could be reversed . <p> He had learnt about the so-called voluntary @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Protocol of 1997 and offered a private sector-led mechanism for companies to offset their emissions by supporting the creation of woodlands . In 2005 , he submitted a proposal for a British version of the VCM to Durham University , which was spotted by a fellow enthusiast , Steve Prior . <p> They made an unlikely couple : Hepburne-Scott , Eton-educated , was an ex-army officer and would-be Tory candidate ; Prior was the former headmaster of a school in Zimbabwe , who had left with his wife for Britain when their small farm was seized . Prior had presented his ideas on carbon capture to a side conference at the 2005 UN Climate Change Conference in Montreal . <p> Between them they set up an initial project to plant four woodlands on the Queensberry estate in Dumfriesshire , aided in part by a grant from Marks &amp; Spencer , then went on to found a joint venture , Forest Carbon , which was sealed with a handshake on the platform of Paddington Tube station in 2006 . Both realised that , alongside tree-planting , the restoration of peatland could @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and in 2022 , as other companies began to take an interest , they organised the UK 's first carbon-financed peatland restoration project in Sutherland , followed by a pioneering peatland programme at Dryhope near Selkirk in the Scottish Borders in 2017 . In the 20 years since its creation , Forest Carbon has supported the creation of some 275 woodlands , putting 13 million trees into UK and Irish soil where they would otherwise not have been planted , and restoring more than 1,400 hectares of degraded peatland . <p> James Patrick Hepburne Scott was the eldest of three children , whose father , Francis , was a farmer and land agent . Their mother , Marjorie Ross , was a direct descendant of Hercules Ross , a Scottish merchant , friend of Horatio Nelson and campaigner for the abolition of the slave trade . Hepburne Scott 's early childhood was spent on the Clandeboye estate near Belfast , where his father was land agent , then Wales , followed by a period on the Eridge estate near Tunbridge Wells . Finally , his father bought the Cardon @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ holidays riding ponies in the hills , and canoeing on the River Tweed -- a stretch of water he loved throughout his life , and which culminated in his five years as the chairman of the Tweed Forum , which manages the restoration of the river . <p> Educated at Aysgarth School in North Yorkshire and Eton College , Hepburne Scott learnt to play the violin , and at Eton joined a reels band that played for dances at the Caledonian Society ; it went on to become the well-known Pictish Players . <p> He went to Sandhurst , where he passed out as a senior under officer , and was said to be on par for the Sword of Honour , a bid somewhat undermined after he fell asleep on his final exercise with his rifle outside his sleeping bag -- judged a Sandhurst cardinal sin at the time . Commissioned into the 1st Battalion of the Black Watch , he served in Germany and Edinburgh , and in 1968 was picked for the royal guard at Balmoral , before reading for a degree in combined science at the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Black Watch continued until 1977 , including three tours of duty in Northern Ireland and two years in Hong Kong . His final military job was as adjutant at the Scottish infantry training depot in Aberdeen . <p> On leaving the army he embarked on a 12-month agricultural course at the Royal Agricultural College Cirencester , followed by four years as a regional sales manager at Rank Hovis McDougall , where he worked with farmers across south Gloucestershire and north Wiltshire , and started to understand the business of farming and estate management . In 1982 , he became a director at a grain company in Kinross and latterly Dundee docks , buying grain from Scotland and Northumberland . <p> In 1968 , at the 21st birthday party of his cousin Andrew , he met Christian Surtees , the younger sister of Andrew 's fianc ? e , and they were married in London in 1972 . Theirs was a happy marriage which was to last for 53 years . They had three children : Walter , a civil servant and co-founder of the MoD 's " defence green @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an entrepreneur and funder of BundleBean , which makes waterproof wear for babies and toddlers ; and George , a chartered surveyor and director of Forest Carbon . They lived in Gloucestershire , before buying a 220-acre farm in Lauderdale , in the Borders , and building their house Larkhill , where they lived and farmed for 28 years . In 2021 they moved to Pewsey in Wiltshire . Three years later he was diagnosed with a glioblastoma ; his wife and three children survive him . <p> In 1990 , Hepburne Scott , whose uncle was Lord Polwarth , a former Scottish Office minister , decided to essay a political career , becoming a prospective Tory candidate for Berwick and East Lothian , but failing to unseat the Labour member for the constituency , John Home Robertson . By now he was heavily involved in the forestry business as sales director for Alba Trees , then later chairman of the Forestry and Timber Association . <p> With the establishment of Forest Carbon , he and Prior were able to demonstrate a holistic approach to land management . They developed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of the carbon that would be captured over the life of a woodland , based on a range of variables . It included a substantial margin for error , so that a tree would sequester more carbon than credits sold . The key to Forest Carbon projects was the concept of " additionality " -- clear evidence that without the carbon finance , the woodland or peatland project could not have progressed . <p> Keen to establish a competitive market for woodland carbon , Hepburne Scott and Prior lobbied the Forestry Commission to develop a government-backed standard . They were instrumental in the development and piloting of the woodland carbon code , launched by the government in 2011 , setting out standards for species mix , enhancing biodiversity , public recreation and , crucially , the criteria for additionality . They then supported Defra on a pilot project focused on unlocking private funding for peatland restoration . It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald . <p> For centuries , the towns and villages of East Lancashire have faced flooding caused by tidal flows moving upstream from the sea and excessive rainfall rushing downstream . <p> A series of flood defences has helped reduce this risk over the years , but as communities expand and climate change brings more extreme weather , many of these defences are reaching the end of their design life and now need repairing , replacing , or extending . <p> To address this challenge , the Environment Agency is delivering the Preston and South Ribble Flood Risk Management Scheme ( FRMS ) , which will provide improved flood protection for around 5,000 homes and businesses . <p> While Ribble Rivers Trust is not directly responsible for constructing the defences , the Trust is supporting the scheme by delivering Biodiversity Net Gain ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for nature as well as people . <p> As part of the scheme , some trees have had to be removed to make way for the new engineered flood defences . <p> To offset these losses , Ribble Rivers Trust has transformed Fishwick Bottoms , a much-loved green space on the banks of the River Ribble , into a thriving new riverside woodland . <p> Located just across the water from Walton-le-Dale and close to Preston city centre , Fishwick Bottoms forms part of the Ribble Free Stretch , a popular location for anglers , as well as the Ribble Way , a 72-mile walking route from the estuary to the river 's source at Ribblehead in North Yorkshire . <p> ( Image : Ribble Trust ) Over the past year , Ribble Rivers Trust has planted 11,800 native trees along a 2km stretch of the Ribble at Fishwick Bottoms , roughly 12 new trees for every one removed during engineering works . <p> The site Invasive non-native plants have been removed , and a new net-zero , rapid-setting concrete has been used for gate installations to reduce environmental impact . <p> This woodland will deliver lasting ecological benefits . It will provide a thriving habitat for insects , mammals , and bird species , improve water quality by filtering out sediments and pollutants before they reach the Ribble , and support migratory fish such as Atlantic salmon , brown trout , and European eel . Coarse fish such as chub , dace , roach , and barbel will also benefit . <p> Woodlands also play a vital role in Natural Flood Management ( NFM ) . As the trees grow , their roots will break up compacted soils , allowing rainfall to soak into the ground rather than running straight into rivers . <p> During storms , the woodland will help slow the flow of water and reduce flooding pressures downstream , complementing the new engineered defences . <p> Most of the tree planting is now complete , with the final touches being added using coir mulch mats at the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ competition from weeds , protect young trees during establishment , and avoid the use of plastic guards , which are particularly unsuitable in flood-prone areas where they can be washed away . <p> Fishwick Bottoms is now set to grow into a flourishing riverside woodland that offsets tree loss from the flood scheme , creates vital new habitats , and helps protect East Lancashire homes from flooding for generations to come . <h> follow us <p> This website and associated newspapers adhere to the Independent Press Standards Organisation 's Editors ' Code of Practice . " <p> THE EXPLAINER <h> When does autumn begin ? <p> The UK is experiencing a " false autumn " , according to the Met Office , as leaves turn brown and berries ripen weeks ahead of the official start of the season . Trees and plants began showing autumnal signs in August due to " the stress of extreme summer conditions " , the weather agency said . <p> More scientifically , when a season begins can be defined in three ways : meteorological , astronomical and phenological . Across the Northern Hemisphere , meteorological autumn begins on 1 September and ends on 30 November . Using set calendar periods makes it easier for meteorological and environmental agencies to compare data over years . <p> The astronomical date varies between 21 and 24 September , in time with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ equal length , and ends with the winter solstice in December . <p> The phenological definition relies on the natural world and its response to weather and climate . In the UK , autumn starts when observable events such as leaves falling from trees and the migration of birds begin . Weather and climate conditions mean it varies from year to year . <p> How is climate change affecting the seasons ? Global warming has changed both the length and timing of the seasons , with Europe and the rest of the Northern Hemisphere experiencing a " much more pronounced change in seasonality " than that in the Global South , Jadu Dash , an environmental sciences professor at Southampton University , told Polytechnique Insights . Autumn has started to arrive , on average , two weeks later , while spring arrives a fortnight earlier . <p> Met Office analysis found that for every 1C increase in October temperatures , the date at which trees lose all their leaves is delayed by two or three days . @@128921409 <h> Why wild venison is a climate-friendly swap for beef <p> One million deer roam Scotland -- a number that has doubled since 1990 ( Credit : Getty Images ) <p> In countries like Scotland where deer populations are culled , eating wild venison can be a low-carbon option . <p> My last meat feast was seven years ago . My parents ? were visiting me in London from Costa Rica and we spent the evening going through the brief but rich menu of a small steak restaurant . Meat -- a high-carbon food -- features on my plate for special meals , like my @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ rare occasion I really crave something like the Costa Rican pork belly-based specialty chifrijo . <p> Each person has their own approach to climate-friendly food ; mine is to reduce food-related emissions , not to have a perfect vegetarian scorecard . <p> Since I moved to Scotland a few years ago , a new wrinkle has appeared : venison -- the meat from deer . Deer populations are out of hand here : the Scottish Government estimates that the overall population could be around one million , up from half a million in 1990 . Deer are thriving , partly because humans eradicated their predators , such as wolves and lynx centuries ago . <p> But , was it ? This question was on my mind when I was dining at a cosy pub in Mallaig in the Scottish Highlands and spotted venison steak on the menu . Could wild deer really feature in a climate-conscious diet ? <p> Getty Images <p> Wild venison has a small carbon footprint , as long as hunters do n't travel a long way to cull the deer ( Credit : Getty Images ) @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hunted in US , it was the equivalent of over 3% of all meat consumption nationally . They then asked themselves by how much the country could reduce its meat-related emissions if those hunters swapped shop-bought beef or chicken for their prey ( 90% of them deer and their relatives ) . <p> Their conclusion ? The emissions ' reduction was equivalent to removing 400,000 cars from the road each year . <p> " The main reason being is that if you harvest deer from the wild as a food source , there is little or no habitat destruction , " Moran explains , " unlike what is involved in raising meat on farms " . <p> Moran 's argument rings true , but the answer gets messier the deeper you look . Venison can be a low-carbon option if the deer are not farmed and truly wild . As a meal , wild venison can have a small carbon footprint , as long as hunters do n't travel a long way to cull the deer . <h> Estimating the climate impact <p> Venison can form part of climate-friendly diets @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ when considered on a global scale . <p> " The problem is scale , " says Hannah Ritchie , deputy editor and lead researcher at Our World in Data , an organisation that makes scientific data accessible and understandable , and a global development researcher at the University of Oxford in the UK . <p> " Yes , it might be a reasonable -- and low-carbon -- choice for a small percentage of the UK population to eat wild venison , but the numbers just do n't work for any critical mass of people , " she says . <p> To explore this question , I started with a simpler one : how can one know if something you 're eating contributes to climate change ? <p> When forests or grasslands are cleared to make way for grazing fields and for crops that become animal feed , they release carbon dioxide to the atmosphere . When cows digest food , they naturally produce masses of methane , a potent warming gas . And then there 's the fuel used to transport cattle to fields and slaughterhouses , the energy used @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in the process . <p> Take all the greenhouse gas emissions associated with beef and divide them by how many burgers you can produce , and you have your carbon footprint per burger . <p> To produce 100 grams of protein from beef ( scientists often use protein as a handy equivalent to compare different foods ) , on average 25 kg of carbon dioxide equivalent ( CO2e ) is released . Producing the same amount of protein from peas , results in 0.4 kg of CO2e . Tofu releases 1.6kg , chicken generates 4.3kg and pork 6.5kg of CO23 per 100g of protein . <p> What is CO2e ? <p> CO2 equivalent , or CO2e , is the metric used to quantify the emissions from various greenhouse gases on the basis of their capacity to warm the atmosphere -- their global warming potential . <p> The gap between meat and other sources of non-animal protein is high . So , how does the venison steak on the menu at Mallaig compare ? <p> Firstly , I had to make sure that this was wild , and not farmed , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to industrial meat , is that you 're not rearing additional animals in warehouses or pens -- and finding farmed venison on a menu in Scotland is not uncommon , despite the abundant local wild supply . <p> I asked the waitress about this , and she said their venison came from Knoydart , the wild and remote peninsula across the loch from Mallaig . Satisfied , I ordered one . Being wild or not , it turns out , is the first big question . <p> Getty Images <p> Venison 's carbon footprint is lower than that of beef , but higher than chicken and pork ( Credit : Getty Images ) <p> In February 2024 , the Scottish Venison Association commissioned a report to estimate the carbon footprint of country 's wild venison . The authors tracked factors such as the fuel used by vehicles driven by deer managers and by hunters , the energy used in the processing facility and the methane released by deer themselves . Deer are ruminant animals , just like cows , sheep and goats . This means they have more than one @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ food . Methane is a highly potent gas , which , although shorter-lived in the atmosphere , has a global warming impact 84 times higher than carbon dioxide ( CO2 ) over a 20-year period . <p> According to the Scottish Venison Association 's report , producing 100 grams of protein from wild venison , generates 11.9kg of CO2e . And while this is not the same method as the study that compared different protein sources , it gives a ballpark estimate : less than beef , but higher than chicken and pork . Hardly a climate-friendly meal . <p> But there 's a big caveat : over 90% of this footprint comes from deer themselves . And this opens a debate between experts doing the bean-counting for greenhouse gas emissions . <p> " There 's a fundamental carbon accounting question : wild deer would exist and produce methane regardless of whether they 're culled for venison -- so should it count ? The cow was bred specifically for human consumption , so her methane ( the largest chunk of a cow 's greenhouse gas output ) is impossible to distance from the burger . <p> In the case of venison , Hirst and others argue that " wild deer populations are not being maintained at these high levels for venison production " . In Scotland , where one million deer roam the country , most wild venison is a byproduct of culling programmes required to protect the Scottish landscape from overgrazing . <p> " These deer would exist -- and emit methane -- regardless of whether @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ food , " says Hirst , who is currently undertaking a PhD focusing on deer and forest management at the University of Edinburgh . <p> Experts like Hirst acknowledge a critique to this idea : that there is nothing natural about deer numbers in Scotland ( and elsewhere where they need culling ) , as they reflect how humans have removed predators , altered their habitat and often fight back against efforts to control populations . <p> But in places where culling takes place , and deer meat is available , would it not make sense to use it ? If we take the view that deer 's methane should not be counted , the climate impact of Scottish venison would be much , much lower than beef , and lower than chicken and pork . According to the Italian study , deer would also be a much more sustainable option than beef , but not quite as climate-friendly as chicken and pork . <p> Once you 've established whether deer is wild or not , one must turn to the hunters as the next big issue . Both in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ non-methane emissions came from the petrol used by hunters and by others in the industry . <p> And the hunters , it turns out , hold the key to making my venison steak low carbon or not . <p> " If you travel a long distance to hunt , then any greenhouse gas savings are probably lost in what is produced by the travel vehicle , " says Moran . <p> By now , I 'm hoping that my steak was the result of a local hunter near Mallaig or Knoydart . Collectively , they culled 140 red deer . <p> According to this study , 71 hunters ( who travelled on average 818km or 508 miles ) went home empty handed . And bad shooters are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Italian researchers put it this way : if these 71 people would have stayed home , the remaining 97 hunters could have killed the 140 red deer , they would not have the burden of the petrol-related emissions of the bad-shooters and the carbon footprint per kilogram of venison would roughly half . <p> Getty Images <p> Venison can be a low-carbon option if the deer are not farmed and truly wild ( Credit : Getty Images ) <p> Should we be more selective about who gets a hunting license to lower venison emissions ? @@128936719 <p> Advanced ecological modeling is giving scientists and policymakers new ways to understand when fragile coastal ecosystems cross the line from resilience to collapse . At the center of this work is environmental scientist Taylor Thomson , whose research demonstrates how mathematical models can quantify the delicate balance between nutrient inputs , keystone species survival , and overall ecosystem stability . <p> Thomson 's master 's research at Waikato University is focused on developing predictive frameworks capable of identifying critical transition points in estuarine systems . His models integrate keystone species dynamics , nutrient fluxes , and sediment processes to forecast when once-healthy ecosystems may shift irreversibly into degraded states . <p> " What I 'm trying to do is make a model using a few keystone species in the environment and we 're influencing them with nutrients and sediments to identify in how many years we expect that proverbial ball to go over the hill , " Thomson explained , describing the mathematical foundation of his predictive approach . <p> The work addresses a long-standing challenge in ecology : how gradual , seemingly manageable changes in environmental conditions can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ detects degradation only after these thresholds have been passed , leaving councils and conservationists with expensive restoration as the only option . <h> Taylor Thomson 's Models Quantify Ecosystem Transitions <p> At the core of Thomson 's framework is mamoni , a clam species that functions as both an indicator and a driver of estuarine health . These clams filter water through sediments , recycle nutrients , and sustain the chemical balance that supports biodiversity . But their sensitivity to rising nitrogen and phosphorus levels makes them especially useful for predicting ecological collapse . <p> By embedding these biological relationships into mathematical models , Thomson moves beyond simple correlations . His framework captures the causal pathways that underlie ecosystem transitions , allowing managers to simulate how systems will respond under different nutrient-loading scenarios . <p> This work draws on extensive field validation . As an environmental monitoring officer with the Waikato Regional Council , Thomson spent years collecting water samples , documenting species abundances , and tracking habitat conditions . These datasets now underpin his models , ensuring predictions are grounded in real-world complexity . <p> A particular strength of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pollution does not always appear immediately in coastal waters ; groundwater transport can delay impacts by years or even decades . Thomson 's approach accounts for these temporal dynamics , coupling hydrological transport mechanisms with biological responses to capture the full trajectory of ecosystem change . <h> Making Complex Science Accessible <p> For all their technical sophistication , Thomson 's models are designed to be accessible beyond academia . Through his involvement with Field-Based STEM , he translates graduate-level research into classroom activities for students across New Zealand . <p> " Field-based STEM opens so many doors to kids and teachers just to experience all these things that they never would otherwise , " Thomson said . His outreach work has seen schoolchildren replicate the same water quality assessments he uses in his research , demystifying ecological modeling by grounding it in hands-on experience . <p> This effort stems from his recognition that science communication is as critical as science itself . During his monitoring work , he often found community members assuming his water sampling was related to COVID-19 testing rather than nutrient pollution , a misunderstanding that underscored @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Thomson 's interdisciplinary training -- combining environmental science with psychology -- shapes his communication strategies . By understanding how people process and retain scientific information , he adapts complex ecological concepts into formats that resonate with students , community groups , and policymakers alike . <h> Bridging Research and Real-World Management <p> Now serving as an Environment Specialist at BHP , Thomson applies his predictive models in industrial contexts , testing how ecological frameworks can inform environmental compliance and management decisions . The role provides a unique opportunity to validate academic research in high-stakes , real-world scenarios . <p> The combination of rigorous modeling and effective communication represents a growing paradigm in environmental science : research that not only advances theory but also equips practitioners with tools for immediate action . <p> As coastal ecosystems worldwide face intensifying pressures from climate change , population growth , and industrial development , the need for such predictive models is only increasing . Thomson 's work offers councils , conservationists , and communities a way to anticipate tipping points before they occur -- shifting environmental management from reaction to prevention .

@@128941931 <h> Red squirrels ' resistant to climate change ' <p> Red squirrels appear to be resilient to climate change in Europe , a new study has found . <p> Scientists at Bournemouth University used climate models to help assess the ability of the species to survive when faced with different climate change predictions . <p> It revealed that temperature changes and lack of rainfall do not have a direct influence on the survivability of red squirrels . <p> Habitat , food availability and disease were found to have more of an impact on the species which , in the south of England , has been confined to islands such as the Isle of Wight and Brownsea Island in Dorset . <p> The native species have largely been wiped out in the UK following the introduction of grey squirrels from the US in the 19th Century . <p> Red squirrels ' diet is mainly made up of tree seeds , supplemented with insects , fungi and birds ' eggs . <p> They live in coniferous forests and deciduous wood across Europe from Spain , Italy , northern Greece , Scandinavia and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ means they can live in a range of climates . <p> The Bournemouth University study investigated how well the population coped with temperature changes and low rainfall . <p> Alyson Buchanan , conservation biologist and ecological researcher said the modelling showed they had " natural ability to adapt to a range of climatic conditions " where food sources might be limited . <p> " We can see that red squirrel populations are not directly affected by current climate patterns in the models . <p> " Other factors such as habitat , food availability , disease and competing species appear to matter more and underline the need to maintain positive conservation efforts for this well-loved species . " <p> Red squirrels have suffered in competition with the larger , heavier and hungrier grey squirrel who will usually win the fight for food . <p> The greys also carry the squirrelpox virus , which is fatal to the red species . <p> However , the population on the Isle of Wight has survived as the Solent acts as barrier , preventing grey squirrels coming into contact with them .

Proportionality and purpose are established cornerstones of data gathering . " <p> Families can help @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ways to help protect blackbirds in your garden <p> Make sure to clean all bird feeders and feeding stations at least once a week to reduce the risk of disease transmission amongst birds . <p> If you spot any sick or dead birds , it 's vital to report it to Garden Wildlife Health or the Animal and Plant Health Agency ( APHA ) , as early reporting helps in tracking outbreaks like Usutu . Ecologists are encouraging families to make small changes that could significantly help protect one of our most beloved garden birds . <p> Data first revealed in June showed a 40% decline in blackbirds in Greater London since the virus was first detected in 2020 - and with climate change assisting mosquitoes in expanding their range , experts warn that the problem is only set to worsen . The Usutu virus , transmitted by the Culex pipiens mosquito - also known as the house mosquito - poses no threat to humans in the UK , but often proves lethal to birds - especially blackbirds , who are particularly prone to infection . <p> With prolonged summers , rising temperatures and heavier rainfall creating ideal breeding conditions for mosquitoes , ecologists caution that climate change is allowing diseases like Usutu to establish a foothold in the UK for the first time . <p> The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ population and further declines in some species are expected unless steps are taken to mitigate additional pressures such as habitat loss and food scarcity . <p> Ecological experts at Arbtech are now urging families to support one of Britain 's most common garden visitors , whose numbers are under threat . <p> A spokesperson for Arbtech said : " Blackbirds are more than just a familiar visitor to our gardens - they 're important seed dispersers and insect predators , helping to regulate pest populations and support healthy ecosystems . <p> " But they 're under real pressure . Diseases like Usutu virus , which can cause tremors , disorientation and even sudden death in infected birds , are an emerging threat - and many people still do n't realise the impact it 's already having . <p> " The good news is that households with even a small garden can make a real difference . Simple actions like planting native shrubs , providing clean water and avoiding pesticides all help create safer , healthier habitats for blackbirds to feed , nest and thrive . " <p> Families can help @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Seven methods to help safeguard blackbirds in your outdoor space <p> Make sure to cleanse all bird feeders and feeding stations at least once weekly to reduce the chance of disease spreading between birds . <p> Should you spot any unwell or dead birds , it 's vital to notify Garden Wildlife Health or the Animal and Plant Health Agency ( APHA ) , as prompt reporting helps monitor outbreaks such as Usutu . The signs of the Usutu virus in blackbirds can differ , but affected birds frequently display indicators of serious neurological and physical distress . <p> Common signs include sluggishness or frailty , lack of coordination , wobbly movement , confusion or strange behaviour ( like failing to escape from humans ) , shaking , fits , and puffed-up plumage - a typical indication of sickness in birds . Think about making wildlife corridors by leaving spaces in fences or planting hedgerows to help blackbirds and other species move safely between gardens .

@@128975313 <p> Labour has developed a sordid partnership with the fossil fuel industry for a dirty-energy future . <p> A basic contradiction runs through UK climate policy . On the one hand , the government accepts that oil and gas extraction will increase , and that domestic uses will increase . It even promotes more airports and roads , thus intensifying climate vandalism . <p> On the other hand , ministers claim that their policy favours clean energy for decarbonisation , and progress towards Net Zero Emissions . That claim should and does provokes suspicion , for many reasons beyond climate issues alone . <p> Keir Starmer promised to extend the left-wing Corbyn agenda through his 10 Pledges to become Labour Party leader in 2020 . But he gradually abandoned most of them , even before the July 2024 general election . <p> Vandalism <p> Since then , the Labour government has provided pale versions of its only worthwhile commitments , maintained low-rate taxes for the wealthiest , and imposed welfare cuts on the most vulnerable people , supposedly necessary to avoid a large budget deficit . <p> Critics as a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ now many go even further and call this government ' worse than the Tories ' . The term ' betrayal ' now seems a gross understatement . <p> Despite the government 's wider disrepute and climate vandalism , its general dirty-energy policy has hardly been contested by climate campaigns , including NGOs and activist groups . Instead they focus on specific issues . <p> Although all those demands are necessary , it leaves open the question - why such a narrow , fragmented approach ? Given the government 's core policy , why is opposition difficult ? <p> In this article I will argue that the Labour government has lulled some climate campaigns through a narrative combining three related promises : that novel decarbonisation technologies plus more renewable energy will achieve Net Zero Emissions ( NZE ) . These three deceptions together maintain a mirage of a low-carbon , green transition . <p> They warrant critical scrutiny , as a crucial basis to counterpose a true decarbonisation agenda within a just transition . Let 's examine each deception in turn . <p> Labour has developed a sordid partnership with the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ future scenario provides a rationale to rebrand - and so perpetuate - natural gas as a ' transition fuel ' for the foreseeable future . <p> Western governments ( among others ) have embraced this narrative in recent years , thus postponing efforts to phase out fossil fuels . State research programmes for energy futures internalise and legitimise those assumptions of the fossil fuel industry . <p> The flagship technofix , Carbon Capture Use and Storage ( CCUS ) , will supposedly break down natural gas into CO2 , which will be stored , and hydrogen , which can be used as a low-carbon fuel , and be flexibly stored or transported through natural gas infrastructure . <p> This technological promise lacks a credible track record ; it remains to demonstrate feasibility on a large scale . <p> In its most feasible and profitable form to date , CCUS has provided CO2 for Enhanced Oil Recovery . Here , it is pumped into oil reservoirs to increase the pressure and make them easier to extract . This method facilitates , and so incentivises , extraction , increasing carbon emissions . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ research and development funds for oil companies to develop CCUS . <p> With its false promise , they have allowed the industry to expand extraction of fossil fuels , even continuing their subsidies . TheCarbon Coup , the report from Corporate Europe Observatory published last year , shows how a fossil fuel agenda has shaped EU policy and its official expert advice . <p> The UK has undergone an analogous shift . Before the Labour Party gained power in the UK , it had promised a ? 28 billion annual fund for green industries . This included substantial funds to retrofit buildings and instal insulation , thus cheapening warm homes and avoiding energy wastage . <p> After the 2024 election , the Labour government drastically reduced the figure , while allocating most of it to CCUS rather than other uses that would bring people faster benefits . <p> As George Monbiot argued , the UK 's CCUS schemes will impose unlimited financial liabilities and huge environmental costs , while contributing little to decarbonisation . Moreover , it will help dirty energy to marginalise renewable energy , as we argued in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Britain 's largest single source of carbon emissions , which result from burning wood pellets . Their ' renewable ' status has made the plant eligible for enormous subsidies , which will continue under the Labour government . But this status is much disputed . <p> Moreover it has authorised Drax to fit CCUS technology , which will increase the costs while bringing doubtful carbon reductions , much less a low-carbon energy source . Nevertheless CCUS helps to protect the company 's investment and to justify the subsidy . <p> In response , all environmental campaigns should demand that the UK government cease funding CCUS , including ' research ' investigating the wrong questions . <p> Those efforts reinforce local resistance campaigns . For many years the HyNet CCUS project in northeast England has been opposed by the HyNot campaign . <p> Perpetuate <p> In August 2025 this escalated with a legal challenge : " HyNot is challenging HyNet in the courts because we believe the scheme will lock the country into continued fossil fuel use and undermine energy security through continued reliance on imported gas . HyNet wo n't @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ countries have likewise been greenwashing their fossil fuel expansion through CCUS technology . In 2024 the Labour government agreed to help Saudia Arabia to do just this , in the hope that it will invest some of its vast oil wealth in the UK 's own techno-fixes . For this partnership , the UK deploys its false image of " climate leadership " . <p> The supporters of nuclear power , a different kind of techno-fix , also portray it as a means to increase low-carbon clean energy supply . <p> This claim too involves many deceptions . Beyond familiar disputes over safety and waste disposal , the UK civil nuclear programme has always been driven by the nuclear weapons programme - especially the need for plutonium . Thus nuclear energy and nuclear armament has been a somewhat false distinction . See the critique by Andy Stirling and Philip Johnstone . <p> Given the long timescale before any new energy production from nuclear power , its pretensions likewise serve to perpetuate fossil fuels as the default mode , while diverting investment from truly renewable sources . This leads us to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Renewable energy ( RE ) has been expanding in most Western countries . Yet it plays a deceptive role in decarbonisation policy , for several reasons . <p> Globally , electricity usage has been rising faster than renewable sources - which largely supplement fossil fuels , rather than replacing them . <p> Along similar lines , UK energy demand has been rising , especially for electricity . The rise has had several drivers : adoption of electric vehicles ( EVs ) , the electrification of heating systems , energy-intensive industries and the explosion of data centres . <p> Thanks to the way that the wholesale market is regulated , the UK 's energy prices are largely set according to the gas price . That in turn is linked to the oil price ; both gas and oil prices are kept high to facilitate extraction . <p> The future promise of lower prices lacks credibility in people 's experience , thus limiting public support for a decarbonisation policy . <p> Renewable energy installations generally must wait as long as 15 years before gaining a suitable connection to the grid ; @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Even as the supply of renewable energy increases , the overall system may prioritise fossil fuels , which is more profitable for producers and can less easily be turned off than renewable energy sources , especially given the inadequate storage capacity . <p> In all those ways , renewable energy provides a mirage of decarbonisation , largely complementing fossil fuels . Meanwhile the overall rising emissions are disguised or excused , leading us to the third deception . <p> Net Zero Emissions ( NZE ) undermining climate targets <p> The UK government 's Net Zero Emissions ( NZE ) target has undergone attack by various right-wing forces . They raise several criticisms . These include the claims that NZE would be unnecessarily expensive , make energy costs less affordable for lower-income people , and limit future employment in energy industries . <p> As the government has argued , the criticisms are in fact invalid , especially if NZE comes with appropriate support measures for alternative energy and employment . <p> However , this narrow debate has helped the government to greenwash its high-carbon version of NZE , partly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ when there 's sufficient silence from the science and expert community , that any old fluff and nonsense can masquerade as Paris-compliant . Just look at the UK ; more oil/gas/LNG/airport expansion , all net-zero compliant . The expert ( &amp; journalist ) community has failed society on the ' net ' scam . " <p> Decarbonisation <p> Worse than this silence or failure , the state-sponsored Committee on Climate Change ( CCC ) has been actively complicit . Its partisan expertise has incorporated the state 's political assumptions . <p> This includes the claim that lower-carbon behavioural or systemic changes are unthinkable but will be made unnecessary by fantastical technofixes . " Ultimately , the CCC is deeply conservative on near-term changes to consumption norms , while embracing dangerously optimistic projections of future carbon removal technologies , " further argues Anderson . <p> The term NZE originally meant phasing out fossil fuels as far as technically possible , while also cancelling out residual emissions with carbon-removal measures or carbon credits . <p> But Western countries have stretched the original meaning to accommodate a much larger ' net ' figure @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ swapped or removed . <p> The dirty-fuel expansion involves a false dual narrative : that countries can ' overshoot ' the earlier timetable for decarbonisation targets and then catch up later . How ? Through hypothetical technoscientific solutions such as CCUS or geo-engineering . <p> Likewise , in 2021 , three climate scientists raised the alarm : " We have arrived at the painful realisation that the idea of Net Zero has licensed a recklessly cavalier ' burn now , pay later ' approach which has seen carbon emissions continue to soar . It has also hastened the destruction of the natural world by increasing deforestation today , and greatly increases the risk of further devastation in the future . " <p> Consequently , the Net Zero concept has helped kill the Paris Agreement aim of keeping global warming within 1.5 degrees , argues James Dyke , one of those three scientists . <p> Rather than count on a compensatory catch-up , an international network of campaigners has now demanded real solutions to achieve ' real zero ' emissions . This perspective opposes techno-optimist carbon-accounting with its false solutions . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the slogan " system change not climate change " a couple of decades ago . This called for the prompt phasing out of fossil fuels , while changing the economic system that drove them . <p> As such a phase-out became widely advocated , the fossil fuel industry devised ways to protect its financial assets from being devalued . <p> In particular , it rebranded natural gas as a ' transition fuel ' . The industry gained government partners for this deceptive high-carbon agenda . It marginalised efforts towards decarbonisation - never mind system change . <p> Meanwhile it has been greenwashing the effects by combining three deceptions : future techno-fixes reducing carbon emissions , renewable energy replacing fossil fuels , and NZE with justifying a later catch-up . <p> Sordid <p> But why is opposition to this fossil fuel resurgence so difficult ? Here are three plausible reasons . <p> First , the three deceptions together reinforce the mirage of a green or climate transition . Perhaps all this has lulled some climate campaigners and their supporters to miss the big picture of the government 's dirty-energy agenda . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ should " follow the science " , a misnomer for the official expert advice that has been ignored or questioned by right-wing agendas denying anthropogenic climate change . So climate campaigners may be reluctant or unable to challenge ' the science ' , even when it is complicit with techno-optimistic deceptions . <p> Third , a narrow political focus may help to avoid despair . For many years , climate campaigners had expected significant decarbonisation efforts by a future Labour government . Instead , Labour has developed a sordid partnership with the fossil fuel industry for a dirty-energy future - among other harmful policies . <p> Energy-intensive <p> Facing such strong forces , effective opposition may seem difficult and even dangerous , especially given the sweeping criminalisation of climate and peace activists . <p> Rather than despair , it is more comfortable to miss the big picture by focusing on specific demands , which may seem safer and more winnable . <p> Yet this fragmented approach remains politically weak . A true decarbonisation agenda would address all of those limitations and deceptions . <p> In this spirit , we should @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ according to their production cost , connect new renewable sources more rapidly , and prioritise renewable sources over natural gas and cease support for CCUS and nuclear power . <p> Furthermore , the Labour government must promote and incentivise reductions in total energy usage . For example , it could deter energy-intensive installations such as AI centres , while incentivising lower-energy systems with more skilled labour to substitute for higher-energy ones . <p> Transition <p> More fundamentally , governments would favour partnerships and critical expertise for such real solutions rather than for deceptive evasions . <p> To achieve those aims and policies , a political movement for system change will need to confront the systemic profit-driven forces which perpetuate fossil fuels , their clever disguises , their government sponsors and their expert apologists . <p> " The choice is not between populist denial and technocratic greenwash , " Nicolas Beuret and Peter Bloom argue . " The real choice is between deep transformation or ecological and social collapse . " <p> As the UK government perpetuates climate vandalism , prominent experts collude through politically partisan advice , while other experts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ provide political education about the big picture . <p> We need to pose true solutions which can bring forward a socially just , low-carbon transition beyond fossil fuels . Progress will depend on building a politically informed , mass counter-power . Our discussions should focus on how to do so . <p> This Author <p> Les Levidow is a Senior Research Fellow at the Open University . Across the population as a whole , 45 per cent are proud while 15 per cent are ashamed , a net score of 30 . <p> There is a stark gender divide . @@128981796 <h> To repel Putin , Britain and Europe must be ready to punch back hard <p> A weak response to Russian aggression will cost far more in the long term than spending more on defence and doing it quickly <p> General Sir Richard Barrons <p> Saturday September 06 2025 , 6.00pm , The Sunday Times <p> Would European troops be committed to fight alongside Ukrainians if Russia violated a ceasefire ? <p> DIEGO HERRERA CARCEDO/ANADOLU/GETTY IMAGES <p> General Sir Richard Barrons <p> Saturday September 06 2025 , 6.00pm , The Sunday Times <p> The war in Ukraine has become the central test of Europe 's ability to defend itself . Any eventual ceasefire or settlement will matter less for what it promises on paper than for how it is enforced in practice . If the West can not back Ukraine with meaningful guarantees , then peace will be little more than a pause until the next round of fighting . The stakes are not confined to Ukraine 's survival . They cut to the heart of Europe 's security over the next decade and beyond . <p> For Britain , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ strategic defence review ( SDR ) . That document made clear that we have entered a new era of confrontation : state-led conflict in a turbulent world shaped by climate change , population pressures , nuclear proliferation and the disruptive effects of the digital age . The SDR warned that the risks we face are of a wholly different order from the relatively comfortable uncertainties of the post-Cold War era . We are living in a time when deterrence can fail suddenly and catastrophically , and when the cost of weakness is measured not only in lost security but also in lost prosperity and values . <h> High stakes <p> Ukraine today is the front line in this new world . Russia 's invasion has shown the devastating consequences of misjudging deterrence . For the UK , the lesson is that we must recover both the will and the means to defend ourselves , and to play our full part in collective security , particularly through Nato . The Nordic and Baltic countries have long pursued a model of " total defence " -- marshalling society as a whole in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but our response must reflect the same seriousness of purpose . <p> John Healey , the defence secretary , during a visit to Warminster Garrison , Wiltshire , after the announcement of a ? 5 billion investment in innovative capabilities , including drones and directed energy weapons , in June <p> LEON NEAL/PA <p> The SDR laid out a ten-year plan to raise defence spending to 3.5 per cent of GDP , with another 1.5 per cent dedicated to defence-related infrastructure by 2035 . In principle , this is a sound prescription . The problem lies in the assumption that we have ten years to prepare . Events may not grant us that time . If Russia , or another adversary , moves faster , then Britain must be ready to accelerate -- spending more , sooner -- rather than relying on good fortune , American indulgence or the restraint of opponents while we repair our defences . <p> Guaranteeing Ukraine 's future is the defining event . For Ukrainians , the immediate prize is survival as an independent state , free to choose its own path , even if @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and Europe , the larger prize is a new security order that sets firm boundaries on Russian aggression . By contrast , a weakly supported ceasefire would embolden Moscow , signalling that Europe remains indecisive and vulnerable . <p> Advertisement <h> Russia 's calculus <p> President Putin during a convivial meeting with Kim Jong-un in Beijing on Wednesday <p> KOREAN CENTRAL NEWS AGENCY/KOREA NEWS SERVICE/AP <p> Russia is adept at reading weakness . Guarantees that look impressive on paper but collapse at the first sign of strain would invite further aggression . Nato planners are well aware that a Russia allowed to regroup could , within as little as four years , be ready to test the alliance directly . A small but well-resourced incursion against a Nato member might be enough to probe whether Article 5 -- the principle that an attack on one is an attack on all -- still holds in practice . If Nato failed to respond unanimously , the alliance itself could unravel . <p> This risk underscores a deeper strategic absurdity : that 500 million prosperous Europeans continue to rely on 350 million Americans @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ changed since 1949 . It is equally absurd that 140 million Russians , most of them far poorer than their European neighbours , can dictate terms to a continent whose economy is 12 times the size of Russia 's . Europe 's combined defence spending , even at the Nato minimum of 2 per cent of GDP , is already twice what Russia spends by militarising its entire economy . And yet in 2022 , Russia judged -- correctly -- that it could invade Ukraine because western deterrence was weak , divided , and half-hearted . <p> That test is not yet over . <h> What a guarantee must mean <p> So what does a guarantee for Ukraine actually mean ? It can not be limited to training , industrial partnerships , or token patrols in the air and sea . If these measures evaporate the moment Russia breaks a ceasefire , they are guarantees in name only , entirely dependent on Moscow 's consent . History offers no comfort that such arrangements succeed . <p> Advertisement <p> The aftermath of a Russian drone strike on a block of flats @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ A guarantee that collapses at the first breach would be worse than nothing . It would prove that Europe remains fragile and unwilling to endure even limited hardship for its own security . Real deterrence requires the credible ability to fight and , crucially , the will to do so . It requires what strategists call " escalation dominance " : the assurance that if Russia escalates , Europe can escalate further , imposing costs Moscow can not bear . <p> This means that sanctions must be part of the guarantee . Sanctions that truly hurt Russia 's oil-based economy -- not the symbolic measures of past years -- must be readied and imposed , even if they bring uncomfortable consequences at home . Deterrence that avoids hard domestic choices is no deterrence at all . <p> Nor will Russia confine itself to the battlefield in Ukraine . Attacks below the military threshold -- cyber intrusions , disinformation , and covert operations -- will remain part of its strategy . That reality underlines the SDR 's insistence on a " whole of society " approach to defence . Guarantees to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ resilience at home . <h> Signal of resolve <p> Rules of engagement are another critical issue . A guarantee that allows British aircraft to intercept missiles over Ukraine but forbids them from striking the launchers that fired them from Russian territory is not a deterrent . Likewise , a Royal Navy destroyer that can only defend itself in the Black Sea , but not respond if a Ukrainian vessel is attacked , sends a message of weakness . Deterrence must be about the certainty of consequences , not the uncertainty of half-measures . <p> Advertisement <p> The most difficult question is ground forces . Would European troops be committed to fight alongside Ukrainians if Russia violates a ceasefire ? That step would send the strongest signal of resolve and is precisely what Moscow most fears . Stationing Nato troops in Ukraine would prevent Kyiv from resuming offensives , but it would also deny Russia the option of resuming its war at will . <p> Mark Rutte , Nato 's secretary-general , and President Zelensky at a press conference in Kyiv in August <p> DANYLO ANTONIUK/ANADOLU/GETTY IMAGES <h> Long-term commitment <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ other allies were to pledge troops for a fixed three-year period , Russia would simply wait them out . A true guarantee must last until Ukraine is self-reliant in military and industrial terms , and that will take years . The task is not only to equip Ukraine for immediate defence , but to help transform its armed forces along the same digital lines that the SDR prescribes for the UK . <p> For Britain , this will not be cost-free . A long-term commitment could consume the army and Royal Marines , while sustaining parallel obligations such as those in Estonia . The unavoidable conclusion is that Britain may need to expand its forces sooner than budgeted . This will demand political will and public support . But the alternative -- being unprepared when deterrence fails -- would prove far more costly . <h> Risk and reality <p> Some will argue that such guarantees risk direct conflict with Russia . They are right . But the greater risk lies in continuing to posture without acting , hoping that Washington will always step in or that Moscow will show restraint @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the next blow , is not a safe Europe . The way to minimise conflict is not by weakness , but by establishing overwhelming dominance in the language Russia understands best : force . <p> Advertisement <p> A rapid deployment to support a ceasefire will , inevitably , be imperfect . Armies rarely begin wars or interventions at full readiness . What matters is the determination to improve , to adapt , and to stay the course . But the cost of inaction -- of learned fragility and wishful thinking -- is certain to be far higher . <p> Ukraine 's fight is Europe 's fight . If we fail to guarantee its future , we will be gambling with our own . <p> Advertisement <p> General Sir Richard Barrons is a co-author of the strategic defence review and a senior consulting fellow at Chatham House

In the same time period , voters elected a new Senate majority five times and picked a new House majority four times . <p> The only elections this century in which the House , Senate and White House all remained under control of the same party were the only two successful presidential reelection campaigns , for George W. Bush in 2004 and Barack Obama in 2012 . Those are also the only times the same party held on to the White House this century . <p> Today 's politicians have come to expect frequent shifts in power . <p> The last four presidents have all assumed office with unified control of Washington and worked as quickly as possible to exploit it . Barack Obama , Donald Trump , Joe Biden and Trump again in his second term all utilized reconciliation to get around the roadblock of the filibuster in the Senate and pass some sort of sweeping agenda item without help from the other party @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Act . For Trump , it was tax cuts in his first term ; in his second , it was a sweeping tax cut and agenda bill that pared back social safety net spending . For Biden , it was the Inflation Reduction Act , which had a lot more to do with clean energy and climate change than it did with reducing inflation . <p> We 'll see if Trump breaks this mold -- something he is desperatelytryingto do by redrawing congressional maps in search of more Republican seats . But each of those other three administrations immediately lost the House . <p> President George W. Bush defied political gravity and picked up House seats after his first two years in office , but that had a lot to do with his popularity after the 9/11 terror attacks . <p> Bush lost the House four years later , after his reelection , when the public had turned on the wars . <p> Bill Clinton lost the House in his first midterm , the 1994 Republican revolution . It was the first time Republicans had gained control of the House @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ House twice in the years since . <p> Clinton picked up seats in the 1998 midterm , when the country turned against Republican efforts to impeach him . <h> Nationalized elections <p> Sarah Binder , a senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution , said these elections change the balance of power , but a better way to view them is as " nationalized elections . " <p> Voters are less frequently splitting their tickets between a senator or representative from one party and a president from the other as they tend more often to stick with one national party . <p> " We 've had nationalized elections , but we did n't have them back to back to back all the time , " Binder said . <h> Smaller majorities <p> The closes corollary to today is probably the late 19th century , Binder said . <p> " It was similarly a period of high partisanship and ideological disagreement , " she explained , but today there is the added element of much slimmer majorities -- even in presidential elections . Trump , Bush and Clinton all @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ popular vote in their first term . <p> Not all power changes are equal , but they all affect how things work in the US government . <p> If Democrats can wrest control of the House from Republicans next year -- which is more likely than the chance they could flip the Senate -- it will allow them to stand in the way of Trump 's legislative agenda , investigate his administration and gain more power in spending debates . <h> Trump 's popularity matters <p> The general indicator for how a president 's party will do in a midterm election is the president 's own approval rating . Trump 's , as it has been , is underwater . <p> Only twice in the past 20 midterm elections going back to 1938 -- for W. Bush in 2002 and Clinton in 1998 -- has the president 's party not lost seats in a midterm . In both cases , the president had approval ratings over 60% . Today , Trump 's is under 50% . <h> Redrawing maps matters <p> This year , Republicans are trying to change the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ changed the map in Texas to create five new seats to win , although it 's a strategy that might not pay off if groups like Hispanic voters do n't vote with the party in the same way they did in 2024 . <p> Republicans are also looking to redraw maps in Missouri and Ohio . Democrats are stymied by laws and state constitutional obstructions to such shenanigans in many states they control , but they are trying to find seats in California . <h> Every seat could be consequential <p> Democrats of the 1970s and 1980s routinely had 80-plus-seat majorities . @@129035483 <p> Agribusiness and fossil fuel corporations deepen hunger , destroy biodiversity , displace peoples and poison communities - all while profiting from the crisis they created . <p> Livelihoods <p> Against this destruction , food sovereignty offers not only resistance but a real pathway to survival with dignity . It is foundational to climate justice . <p> Food sovereignty was first articulated in 1996 by La V ? a Campesina , the global movement of peasants and rural peoples . Since then , it has been embraced by thousands of organisations and social movements worldwide . <p> The Ny ? l ? ni Declaration of 2007 defines it as " the right of peoples to healthy and culturally appropriate food produced through socially just , ecologically sound and sustainable methods , and their collective right to define their own policies , strategies and systems for food production , distribution and consumption . " <p> In practice , food sovereignty goes well beyond food security . It is a political movement and a living pathway toward transforming the broken food system . <p> It asserts food as a human right , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ life over profit . It defends land , seeds and biodiversity , recognises women 's central role in food production , and demands that peasants , Indigenous Peoples , fisherfolk and smallholder farmers control the decisions shaping their livelihoods and territories . <p> System <p> Understanding why food sovereignty is essential to climate justice means first confronting the role of agribusiness in driving the climate crisis . <p> The global food system , dominated by agribusiness , is today responsible for one-third of greenhouse gas emissions . <p> This model is built on agrocommodities : soy for factory farms , palm oil for processed foods and biofuels , and industrial meat for global supply chains . Its logic is clear : maximise profit through monocultures , chemical inputs and land grabs . <p> By centering peasants and Indigenous Peoples as knowledge holders , it protects seeds , forests and water bodies . <p> Dismantle <p> By rejecting the financialisation of nature , it defends the commons from speculative markets . And this is already being practised by the smallholders , Indigenous Peoples and women who provide between 70 and 80 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ these communities are systemically excluded from policymaking and markets . Decades of neoliberal policies have concentrated power in the hands of a few transnational corporations , so the power imbalance is stark . <p> And while corporations greenwash their destruction with talk of " sustainability " , they push forward false solutions to the climate crisis like geo-engineering , carbon markets and " climate-smart agriculture . " <p> It means rejecting a " green transition " that keeps the inequalities intact , simply swapping fossil fuels for renewables while leaving millions without energy access and maintaining the food system under the control of corporations . @@129036755 <p> On one of the hottest days of the summer , after the warmest spring on record , I -- like many others in the city -- sought refuge from the heat in the shade of my college garden . At the same time , across Cambridge , in wards such as Abbey and Cherry Hinton -- areas with lower average incomes , fewer trees , and limited green space -- residents faced streets of concrete and asphalt that trapped and intensified the heat . While students and staff benefit from the University 's exclusive green spaces , many locals face a starkly different reality . As extreme temperatures become the new norm , a pressing question emerges : who gets to stay cool in Cambridge ? <p> As the UK enters an era of record-breaking temperatures , with the summer of 2025 confirmed as the hottest on record , extreme heat is becoming one of the UK 's most pressing public health threats . High temperatures increase the likelihood of cardiovascular failure , respiratory distress , heatstroke , and dehydration . Data from the UK Health Security Agency shows @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ estimated 2,985 excess deaths , with mortality risk rising sharply once daily maximum temperatures exceed 25 ? C. <p> These health risks are not evenly distributed . The old , the young , and those with chronic illnesses are at heightened risk due to reduced physiological resilience . But vulnerability is not only biological ; it is fundamentally socio-economic . Low-income households often live in poorly insulated homes with limited ventilation , and face barriers to healthcare and higher rates of pre-existing conditions -- all of which increase vulnerability to extreme heat . Racially marginalised communities are also disproportionately exposed ; a 2025 spatial study of Greater London , combining satellite imagery with Census data , found that children , ethnic minorities -- especially Black and Asian populations -- and the lowest-income groups face surface temperatures up to 4 ? C hotter than wealthier , predominantly White neighbourhoods . <p> " Urban areas can be 10-12 ? C hotter than their rural surroundings , driven by the urban heat island ( UHI ) effect " <p> The effects of heat are not just unequal across communities , but across environments @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ government report found that urban areas can be 10-12 ? C hotter than their rural surroundings , driven by the urban heat island ( UHI ) effect , which amplifies extreme temperatures . This phenomenon intensifies where heat-absorbing materials like concrete , tarmac , and glass dominate , as they store far more heat than natural materials like grass or woodland . Surface reflectivity -- or albedo -- also plays a role : dark , low-albedo materials such as asphalt absorb more solar radiation than lighter , reflective ones , while a lack of vegetation limits evapotranspiration ( the natural cooling process where plants release water vapour ) further exacerbating urban heat . <p> Green spaces are crucial to mitigating the UHI effect . The UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology estimates that they can reduce temperatures by 2-5 ? C through shading and evapotranspiration . The communities most vulnerable to heat , due to age , illness , or poverty , are often the same ones living in the hottest , least green parts of our cities . Those areas ranking lowest on the UK Index of Multiple Deprivation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ areas . <p> " Communities most vulnerable to heat , due to age , illness , or poverty , are often the same ones living in the hottest , least green parts of our cities " <p> In Cambridge , this pattern holds : council data shows poorer wards like Abbey and Cherry Hinton have the lowest tree canopy ( 6.8 -- 7.3% ) and little shade , while wealthier areas like Newnham and Trumpington enjoy much more coverage ( 13 -- 18.8% ) . As heatwaves intensify , this overlap of social and environmental vulnerability means the same communities are hit hardest -- twice over . <p> While it 's tempting to imagine climate change exclusively in terms of distant catastrophes -- Tuvalu sinking , melting Arctic ice , Canadian wildfires -- sometimes it 's as innocuous as a hot summer 's day . In an era of rolling heatwaves , access to green space is emerging as a new marker of inequality . So , while our city of gowns and gardens may appear green , it 's high time we ask : green for whom ? <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ University of Cambridge , established in its current form in 1947 . @@129081407 <h> Heavy rain and wind forecast as unsettled weather returns to UK <p> Autumn has arrived and is making its presence known with an unsettled start to September . <p> Wind and rain are set to sweep in from the Atlantic on Wednesday bringing about a drop in temperature and a risk of thunderstorms . <p> The weather will remain unsettled into the weekend with a chance of deeper areas of low pressure developing in the North Atlantic during the coming days <p> Currently it 's too early to be exact about the impact these lows may have - including if any will develop into a named storm . However , as it often the case this time of year , as we transition out of summer and into autumn , we 're now seeing a more westerly influence to the weather . The blocked pattern has broken down and this has opened the doors for Atlantic weather systems to move in . <p> Image caption , <p> Rain is on the way for all of us this week with the wettest weather likely around the western coasts <h> What is the longer range forecast ? <p> As we head deeper into the autumn months , most forecast models indicate an increased chance of a ' wetter than average ' spell from September to November in the UK . However there is always a lot of uncertainty in seasonal forecasts , and these should be interpreted as likely trends rather than expected conditions . <p> It @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ which was the wettest on record for 10 English counties , including Bedfordshire , Buckinghamshire and Wiltshire . They received more than 3 times their expected September rainfall leading to widespread flooding . <h> Will the rain help relieve the drought ? <p> This year so far , the UK has experienced its sunniest spring and warmest summer on record . " . <p> As our world warms , climate scientists expect the UK to experience wetter , warmer winters and hotter , drier summers . @@129081442 <h> When does autumn start ? <p> Image source , Getty Images <p> There are two different answers to when autumn actually starts . <p> The first is called meteorological autumn , where weather scientists divide the year into four exact seasons of three months each . That means autumn always begins on 1 September and ends on 30 November . This makes it easier to compare temperatures , rainfall and sunshine from one year to the next . <p> The other answer is astronomical autumn , which starts at the autumn equinox - usually on 22 or 23 September - and that 's when day and night are almost the same length . After that , days start to become shorter and nights get longer . <h> What is ' false autumn ' ? <p> Image source , Getty Images <p> Sometimes , though , nature seems to go a little early . <p> You may have seen leaves falling in August and conkers dropping weeks earlier than usual . climate change by manipulating the Arctic and Antarctic environment are dangerous , unlikely to work and could distract from the need to ditch fossil fuels , dozens of polar scientists have warned . <p> These polar " geoengineering " techniques aim to cool the planet in unconventional ways , such as artificially thickening sea-ice or releasing tiny , reflective particles into the atmosphere . <p> Net zero means balancing the amount of planet-warming " greenhouse " gases produced by human activities with the amount being actively removed from the atmosphere . <p> But some more radical geoengineering ideas , like reflecting sunlight " are dealing with the symptoms of climate change rather than the causes , " said lead author Martin Siegert , professor of geosciences at the University of Exeter . <p> The scientists behind the new assessment , published in the journal Frontiers in Science , reviewed the evidence for five of the most widely discussed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ criteria for their feasibility and potential environmental risks , they say . <p> One such suggestion is releasing tiny , reflective particles called aerosols high into the atmosphere to cool the planet . <p> This often attracts attention among online conspiracy theorists , who falsely claim that condensation trails in the sky -- water vapour created from aircraft jet engines -- is evidence of sinister large-scale geoengineering today . <p> But many scientists have more legitimate concerns , including disruption to weather patterns around the world . <p> With those potential knock-on effects , that also raises the question of who decides to use it -- especially in the Arctic and Antarctic , where governance is not straightforward . <p> If a country were to deploy geoengineering against the wishes of others , it could " increase geopolitical tensions in polar regions " , according to Dr Valerie Masson-Delmotte , senior scientist at the Universit ? Paris Saclay in France . <p> Another fear is that while some of the ideas may be theoretically possible , the enormous costs and time to scale-up mean they are extremely unlikely to make @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to cover 10% of the Arctic could require about 10 million seawater pumps , one estimate suggests . <p> A more fundamental concern is that these types of projects could create the illusion of an alternative to cutting humanity 's emissions of planet-warming gases . <p> " If they are promoted ... then they are a distraction because to some people they will be a solution to the climate crisis that does n't require decarbonising , " said Prof Siegert . <p> " Of course that would not be true and that 's why we think they can be potentially damaging . " <p> BBC/Jemma Cox <p> One suggestion to save Thwaites Glacier , one of the most vulnerable Antarctic glaciers , is to install a giant sea " curtain " to stop warm water melting it more quickly - but the new study says this would be extremely costly and unlikely to work <p> Even supporters of geoengineering research agree that it is , at best , a supplement to net zero , not a substitution . <p> " The need for emissions reductions comes first ... almost anything @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Dr Shaun Fitzgerald , director of the University of Cambridge 's Centre for Climate Repair , which has been involved in some of the projects highlighted . <p> The assessment raises " very valid concerns " about some of the ideas , but they need to be balanced against the risks from " the perilous state of the climate , " he argued . <p> Like many other supporters of geoengineering research , Dr Fitzgerald does not support deploying it on a large scale yet , and acknowledged that further investigation might indeed find that the ideas are " bonkers " . <p> But he argued that more research would allow society to make " more informed decisions " about whether they could help or hinder in the fight against climate change .

@@129122158 <p> France has recorded nearly 400 locally-acquired cases of chikungunya this summer , a sharp increase from last year , French health authorities announced Wednesday . <p> As of Sept. 8 , there have been 382 cases of chikungunya from infected mosquitoes biting people in mainland France , including 81 from the past week alone , in addition to 966 imported cases . The country also reported 21 cases of locally-acquired dengue and 894 imported cases . <p> It 's a stark increase in the number of chikungunya cases from mosquitoes in the country compared to last year , when only one such case was reported in France . <p> Chikungunya can cause flu-like symptoms , such as high fever , headache , nausea , rash , and muscle and joint pain .
